case_info.scenario: A 3-year-old previously healthy boy presented to the dental office for gum bleeding that developed 2 weeks prior to presentation. His parents reported dark spots on his gums that appeared spontaneously over several days and bleeding during teeth brushing. He had no preceding oral trauma and no recent infections. One week after onset of these oral symptoms, he developed a limp in the right leg. His parents also noticed he had difficulty standing up after sitting down to play. He was evaluated by a pediatrician, who diagnosed transient synovitis of the hip due to a viral infection. Findings on a radiograph of the right hip were normal. During the week prior to presentation, the patient developed spontaneous gingival bleeding and increased bilateral limb weakness with inability to bear weight. On presentation to the dental office, he appeared irritable. Physical examination revealed generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous gingival bleeding. He had no lesions on his lips and no edema or exudate in the oropharynx (Figure). The patient’s parents reported that he took no regular medications, had no recent use of aspirin or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, and that his diet was limited to primarily chicken nuggets and milk.

options.B: Prescribe amoxicillin (125 mg/5 mL oral suspension) for 7 days
options.D: Check plasma level of vitamin C

case_info.explanation: D. Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. The patient’s vitamin C level was undetectable. He started oral vitamin C, 600 mg/d. Within 48 hours, his parents reported resolution of gingival bleeding and improved muscle strength. Two weeks after starting vitamin C, the patient’s gingiva, muscle strength, and gait were normal. He is taking a multivitamin supplement daily, and his parents have incorporated more fruits and vegetables into his diet.

dialogue_history.text: While scurvy is a consideration given the dietary history, the combination of spontaneous gingival bleeding, progressive limb weakness, and a normal hip radiograph in a previously healthy 3-year-old is more concerning for a hematologic malignancy like leukemia. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia often presents with bleeding, gingival hypertrophy, bone pain, and weakness. I would recommend urgent referral to a pediatric emergency department for a complete blood count with differential and peripheral smear first, as this is a higher-yield and faster initial test than vitamin C levels.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: D. Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. The patient’s vitamin C level was undetectable. He started oral vitamin C, 600 mg/d. Within 48 hours, his parents reported resolution of gingival bleeding and improved muscle strength. Two weeks after starting vitamin C, the patient’s gingiva, muscle strength, and gait were normal. He is taking a multivitamin supplement daily, and his parents have incorporated more fruits and vegetables into his diet.

case_info.explanation: D. Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. The patient’s vitamin C level was undetectable. He started oral vitamin C, 600 mg/d. Within 48 hours, his parents reported resolution of gingival bleeding and improved muscle strength. Two weeks after starting vitamin C, the patient’s gingiva, muscle strength, and gait were normal. He is taking a multivitamin supplement daily, and his parents have incorporated more fruits and vegetables into his diet.

       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: D. Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. The patient’s vitamin C level was undetectable. He started oral vitamin C, 600 mg/d. Within 48 hours, his parents reported resolution of gingival bleeding and improved muscle strength. Two weeks after starting vitamin C, the patient’s gingiva, muscle strength, and gait were normal. He is taking a multivitamin supplement daily, and his parents have incorporated more fruits and vegetables into his diet.

case_info.explanation: D. Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. The patient’s vitamin C level was undetectable. He started oral vitamin C, 600 mg/d. Within 48 hours, his parents reported resolution of gingival bleeding and improved muscle strength. Two weeks after starting vitamin C, the patient’s gingiva, muscle strength, and gait were normal. He is taking a multivitamin supplement daily, and his parents have incorporated more fruits and vegetables into his diet.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

case_info.explanation: D. Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. The patient’s vitamin C level was undetectable. He started oral vitamin C, 600 mg/d. Within 48 hours, his parents reported resolution of gingival bleeding and improved muscle strength. Two weeks after starting vitamin C, the patient’s gingiva, muscle strength, and gait were normal. He is taking a multivitamin supplement daily, and his parents have incorporated more fruits and vegetables into his diet.

case_info.explanation: D. Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. The patient’s vitamin C level was undetectable. He started oral vitamin C, 600 mg/d. Within 48 hours, his parents reported resolution of gingival bleeding and improved muscle strength. Two weeks after starting vitamin C, the patient’s gingiva, muscle strength, and gait were normal. He is taking a multivitamin supplement daily, and his parents have incorporated more fruits and vegetables into his diet.

case_info.explanation: D. Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. The patient’s vitamin C level was undetectable. He started oral vitamin C, 600 mg/d. Within 48 hours, his parents reported resolution of gingival bleeding and improved muscle strength. Two weeks after starting vitamin C, the patient’s gingiva, muscle strength, and gait were normal. He is taking a multivitamin supplement daily, and his parents have incorporated more fruits and vegetables into his diet.
